steps: Group your users as representatives, managers and administrators, and plan a hands-on session for each group on your own accounts and prospects.
Train representatives on the prospect and account views, AI Chat and reply suggestions, and on reviewing and approving drafts before any email is sent.
Practice the task queue for calls, LinkedIn InMails and email reviews with representatives: select a task, take action, mark it complete and move to the next one.
Train managers on outbound performance and administrators on the settings, and hand each group a short guide to its routine.
deliverables: Short guides for representatives, managers and administrators
asks: The names and roles of the representatives, managers and administrators to train
Time from each group for the sessions, with their user access already in place
risk: Representatives drifting back to old habits: we train on their own task queue and drafts, and hand each role a short guide to its routine.
outcome: Your representatives work their prioritized prospects and approve outreach in Marketo Qualifier, managers follow outbound performance and administrators keep the settings current.

steps: Review open, click, reply and meeting results in Outbound performance each month, by workflow and by representative, with your sales leaders.
Tune goals and touchpoint prompts, and duplicate and revise the workflows that underperform, keeping each original so results can be compared.
Refresh the Knowledge Center playbook with new sales materials, and record the month's changes and results in a short review note.
deliverables: Monthly outreach review and change log
Revised workflows, goals and touchpoint prompts
asks: A standing monthly slot with your sales leaders to review the results
New sales materials, offers and messaging changes to add to the Knowledge Center
risk: Changes whose effect cannot be told apart: we revise a copy of each underperforming workflow and log every change, so the next review shows what worked.
outcome: Each month your workflows, prompts and Knowledge Center playbook are tuned from reviewed results, with a record of every change made.

steps: Agree with your Workfront administrator who will view and who will create in Workfront Planning, and record each user's license and permissions in an access list.
Assign the Workfront and Planning licenses and the Workfront Planning permissions to each user, and add the license types to their access levels.
Assign a layout template that shows Planning to Contributor and Light users, then test each license type with a sample user before rollout.
deliverables: Access list of users, licenses and permissions
Access levels updated with the license types
Layout template showing Planning to Contributor and Light users
asks: The list of people who will view or create in Workfront Planning
A Workfront administrator to approve the access level and layout template changes
risk: Users who cannot find Planning or can change more than they should: we test each license type with a sample user before rollout.
outcome: Each of your users opens Workfront Planning with the right license and permissions, and Contributor and Light users find Planning in their layout.

steps: Run planning workshops with each team to map its work lifecycle and the things it plans, such as campaigns, products, regions and personas.
Design the workspaces, the record types, their fields and how they connect, including connections to Workfront projects, in a model your team signs off.
Build the workspaces from a predefined template or from scratch, with your own record types, fields and the connections between them.
Test the model with real examples from each team, adjust fields and connections, then share each workspace with the agreed users, groups and teams.
deliverables: Workspaces, record types and fields built
Connections between record types and to Workfront projects
asks: A lead from each team that plans work, for the workshops and sign-off
Your current planning spreadsheets or documents, to show how each team plans today
Decisions on which record types each workspace holds and who owns them
risk: A model that fits one team and not the next: we test it with real examples from every team and adjust it before rollout.
outcome: Your teams plan in Workfront Planning workspaces that match how they work, with campaigns, products and other record types connected to one another.

steps: Collect your planning spreadsheets, agree which ones move, and map each sheet and column to a record type and field in a mapping sheet.
Clean the data with its owners: remove duplicates, align names and values, and fill or flag the gaps before anything is imported.
Import each record type from a CSV or Excel file with its records and fields, starting with a pilot sheet your team checks.
Check the connections between the imported records against the source sheets on a sample, and fix any that did not link.
deliverables: Imported record types, fields and records
asks: Your current planning spreadsheets, with an owner for each one
Decisions on duplicate or conflicting records, from the people who own the data
risk: Duplicates and mismatched names breaking connections: we clean and align the data before import and test a pilot sheet first.
outcome: Your existing plans are in Workfront Planning as records with their fields and connections, so teams start from current data, not empty workspaces.

steps: Agree with your teams and leaders which views each audience needs, such as a marketing calendar or a campaign timeline, and the fields each one shows.
Build the table, timeline and calendar views, with the filters, groupings and fields each audience needs.
Review each view with its audience on real records, and adjust the filters and groupings before handing it over.
Share each view with its audience, since views are shared separately from the workspace, and check that each person sees the intended records.
deliverables: Shared table, timeline and calendar views
asks: The teams and leaders who will use each view, and what they need to see
Time from each audience to review its views on real records
risk: Views that show too much or too little: we build each one for an agreed audience and review it with that audience on real records.
outcome: Your teams and leaders each open a shared view, such as a marketing calendar or campaign timeline, showing the records and fields they need.

steps: Agree which record types you take requests for, the fields each request form asks for, and who approves which requests.
Create a request form for each agreed record type, and add approval rules by field value so each request reaches the right approver.
Test sample requests through every approval rule, then share each form with the people who submit to it.
Hand over a short guide to submitting and approving requests, with the list of forms, rules and approvers.
deliverables: Request forms for the agreed record types
Test results and a short request guide
asks: The record types you take requests for, and who submits each one
The approvers for each kind of request, and the field values that route to them
risk: Requests that reach the wrong approver or none: we test sample requests through every approval rule before the forms are shared.
outcome: Requests arrive as complete records through one form per record type, and each goes to its approver by the rules you agreed.

steps: Agree the questions each leader needs answered from Planning records, and whether each report belongs in the Workfront Canvas Dashboard or your own reporting tool.
Build the agreed reports on your Planning records in the Workfront Canvas Dashboard, laid out around the questions each audience asked.
Prepare the Planning data in Workfront Data Connect where reports belong in your own tool, and agree the fields your reporting team receives.
Check each report's figures against the records in Workfront Planning, and walk each audience through its reports.
deliverables: Reports in the Workfront Canvas Dashboard
Planning data in Workfront Data Connect, where used
asks: The questions your leaders want answered from planning data
A contact for your own reporting tool, if reports will be built there
risk: Reports that disagree with the records: we check each report's figures against Workfront Planning before handing it over.
outcome: Your leaders follow planning in reports built on your Planning records, in the Workfront Canvas Dashboard or in your own reporting tool.

steps: Plan the rollout team by team, with an order, a start date and a named lead for each team, in a rollout plan.
Teach each team the Planning terms first, since Workfront Planning has its own concepts and terminology, even for people who know Workfront.
Train each team to add, connect and view records in its own workspace, with exercises on its own plans.
Hand over a short guide for workspace owners, and walk each owner through it before their team starts.
asks: A lead from each team to set its dates and gather its people
Time from each team for training in its own workspace
risk: People who know Workfront assuming Planning works the same way: we teach the Planning terms first and practice in each team's own workspace.
outcome: Each team adds, connects and views its own records in Workfront Planning, and workspace owners have a guide for everyday upkeep.

steps: Gather change requests from workspace owners each month, and add the record types, fields and views your planning now needs.
Tidy records and connections with their owners, removing duplicates and stale records and fixing connections that no longer link.
Adjust sharing for people who join, move or leave, and send a monthly note of the changes made.
deliverables: Monthly changes to record types, fields and views
asks: A workspace owner in each team to send change requests each month
Notice of people joining, moving or leaving the teams that use Planning
risk: A model that drifts as teams add fields on their own: we make every change from one request list and record it in the monthly note.
outcome: Your Workfront Planning model keeps pace with how you plan, with clean records, working connections and sharing that matches your teams.

steps: Run use-case workshops with your marketing, data and privacy leads, and rank the use cases the first release must support.
List your entities and sources in an inventory, and map each entity into profile, event and lookup schemas against the ranked use cases.
Choose the identity namespaces and primary identities the profile will merge on, such as a CRM ID or a hashed email, with your data team.
Flag sensitive attributes and their data-use rules in the design, test the chosen identities on sample records, and take the model to sign-off.
deliverables: Schema design for profile, event and lookup data
asks: Marketing, data and privacy leads for the use-case workshops
Sample records and field lists from each source system
A decision owner for the identifiers your systems share
risk: Profiles that merge the wrong people or fail to merge: we test the chosen identities on sample records from each source before sign-off.
outcome: You have a signed-off data model and identity design for the build to follow, tied to the use cases you ranked first.

steps: Agree the sources, such as CRM, loyalty, commerce and web or app events, with each system owner, and record access and refresh needs in a source inventory.
Connect each agreed source, whether an Adobe application, cloud-based storage or a database, starting with one pilot source end to end.
Map each source's fields to XDM in a mapping sheet your data team signs off, including the person-level identifier each source carries.
Enable the datasets for Profile, run the first loads, and check that they build the expected profiles against record counts from each source.
Reconcile a sample of profiles with each system owner, fix any mapping gaps, and record how each source loads in a runbook for your team.
deliverables: Source inventory and XDM mapping sheet
asks: An owner for each source system who can grant access and answer field questions
Sample extracts from each source, with the identifiers each one carries
Sign-off on the field mapping from your data team
risk: Loads that look complete but build the wrong profiles: we pilot one source end to end and check counts and sample profiles before adding the rest.
outcome: Your agreed sources load into Experience Platform with mapped fields, building the customer profiles your audiences and use cases depend on.

steps: Agree with your data team which source wins when values conflict, and record the dataset order and the reason for each choice.
Set the merge method and dataset priority in the default merge policy, following the agreed order.
Review how the identity graph links records, flag people joined by shared or test identifiers, and agree the fixes with your data team.
Check a sample of profiles against the source data, field by field, and record the results before audiences are built on them.
asks: A data team lead to decide which source wins for each attribute
Access to the source records behind the sample profiles we check
risk: Profiles that join different people: we review how the identity graph links records and check sample profiles against source data before audiences use them.
outcome: Each customer profile in Experience Platform shows values from the right sources, by the rules your data team agreed.

steps: Agree the starting audiences with your marketing team, write each one's rules in an audience sheet, and build them on the profile data.
Connect the agreed destinations, such as the Adobe Target destination, and choose the identities and attributes each receives, leaving out sensitive attributes unless you approve them.
Schedule the first activations and test each one end to end, checking audience counts and a sample of profiles in the receiving system.
Record each audience, destination and schedule in an activation register, and show your team how to add the next audiences.
deliverables: Connected destinations with agreed identities and attributes
asks: The starting audiences and the channels each one feeds
Access and a contact for each destination platform
Approval for any sensitive attribute a destination will receive
risk: Sending more data than a use needs: we agree the identities and attributes for each destination, and Experience Platform enforces the data usage policies you enable at activation.
outcome: Your starting audiences reach the agreed destinations on schedule, carrying only the identities and attributes each use needs.

steps: Agree roles and permissions with your administrators, and set up development and production sandboxes, so building and testing stay apart from live data.
Apply schema-field usage labels with your privacy team, marking sensitive attributes and any field with limits on where it may be sent.
Enable the agreed data usage policies, and test sample activations to show each policy is enforced before any live audience is sent.
Record roles, sandboxes, labels and policies in a governance record that your administrators keep current.
deliverables: Labeled schema fields and enabled data usage policies
Governance record and policy test results
asks: A list of users from your administrators, with what each one may do
A privacy lead to agree the usage labels and data usage policies
risk: A sensitive field reaching a destination it should not: we label fields before activation and test each policy on sample activations.
outcome: Your team builds and tests apart from production, with the right access for each role, and activations follow the data usage policies you agreed.

steps: Review the source and destination dataflows and alerts each month, and fix failed runs with the owners of the systems involved.
Retire audiences no one uses and refresh the rest with your marketing team, keeping the audience list current.
Add destinations as new use cases come in, with the identities and attributes agreed for each one.
Report the month's dataflow health, fixes and audience changes to your team in a short monthly note.
deliverables: Log of failed runs and fixes
asks: A contact in each source and destination system to help fix failed runs
New use cases from your marketing team, with the audiences and channels they need
risk: A failed run that leaves audiences stale: we review dataflows and alerts each month, fix the cause with the system owner and log it.
outcome: Your data keeps flowing into Experience Platform and out to destinations, with audiences kept current and new use cases added each month.

steps: Review the month's new SEO opportunities in Sites Optimizer with your content owner, and approve or edit each suggested fix.
Deploy approved content fixes into authoring and hand code patches to your named developer; with Prime, apply content and configuration fixes by hand and pass code recommendations to the developer.
Log each fix's route and status, and report search traffic and Core Web Vitals movement in the monthly Brand Visibility review.
deliverables: Monthly fix log with each fix's route and status
Content fixes in authoring, ready to publish
Code patches or recommendations handed to your named developer
Monthly search traffic and Core Web Vitals report
asks: A content owner to approve or edit the suggested fixes each month
A named developer to review, test, merge and release the code patches
risk: A code patch that breaks the site: every patch goes to your named developer to review and test through your own release process before it merges.
outcome: Each month's approved SEO fixes are in authoring or with your developer, logged with their status, and you see search traffic and Core Web Vitals movement.

steps: Agree the pages, activity types and data Target needs with your web and analytics teams, and record them in an implementation plan.
Enable Target in the datastream and add flicker handling, testing it on your key pages so default content does not flash before an experience appears.
Render Visual and Form-based Experience Composer activities, and pass the profile and entity data your activities and audiences will use.
Validate the setup with test activities on each page type, checking that experiences render and data arrives, and record the results in a validation log.
deliverables: Target enabled in the datastream, with flicker handling
Profile and entity data passed to Target
Validation log with test activity results
asks: A web developer who can deploy changes to your site's pages
The pages and data your first activities will need, agreed with your marketing team
risk: Visitors seeing default content flash before an experience appears: we add flicker handling and test it on your key pages before any activity goes live.
outcome: Target is enabled on your pages, ready for A/B tests and Experience Targeting activities built in the Visual or Form-based Experience Composer.

steps: Agree with your Target administrator who does what in Target, then add your users and assign their roles from the agreed access list.
Create workspaces, user groups and properties where you have Target Premium, and add the at_property parameter to your Target implementation.
Set up the reporting, environment and starting audience settings, and test them with a sample activity before your first live test.
Record users, roles, workspaces, properties and settings in an administration record your team keeps current.
deliverables: Workspaces, user groups and properties, where used
Reporting, environment and starting audience settings
asks: The people who will use Target, and what each one will do
A Target administrator to approve roles and workspace access
risk: Teams changing each other's activities: we agree roles, workspaces and properties before the first activity is built, and test access with each role.
outcome: Your team works in Target with the right roles, workspaces and settings in place, ready to build its first activities.

steps: Run an ideation and prioritization workshop with your marketing, product and analytics leads, and rank ideas by business alignment, level of effort and potential impact.
Write an activity plan for each top idea, with its hypothesis, audience, success metrics and the decision a result will drive.
Build the first A/B and Experience Targeting activities, and QA each one across pages, devices and audiences before launch.
Launch the first activities once each passes QA and its plan is signed off, and hand each plan and QA record to the team that will read its results.
deliverables: Activity plans with hypotheses and success metrics
First live A/B and Experience Targeting activities
asks: Marketing, product and analytics leads for the ideation and prioritization workshop
Sign-off on each activity plan and its success metrics before build
risk: Tests that end without a clear answer: every activity plan sets its hypothesis and success metrics before build, so each result drives a decision.
outcome: You have a ranked testing roadmap and your first A/B and Experience Targeting activities live, each with a plan that defines success.

steps: Agree whether you recommend products or content, on which key pages, and the catalog attributes the recommendations will draw on.
Set up the product or content catalog feed, and check a sample of items against your source catalog after the first load.
Pass item, category and cart data on the key pages with your web developers, and test that each page sends the expected values.
Set the global exclusions and Recommendations settings, review the first recommendations with your merchandising or content team, then launch them.
deliverables: Item, category and cart data on key pages
asks: A catalog owner who can supply the product or content feed and answer attribute questions
A web developer to add item, category and cart data to key pages
The items or categories that must never be recommended
risk: Items you never want shown appearing in recommendations: we set the global exclusions first and review the first recommendations with your team before launch.
outcome: Your key pages show recommendations drawn from your product or content catalog, within the global exclusions you set.

steps: Pick the next activities from the roadmap each month with your team, and write each one's plan with its hypothesis and success metrics.
Design, build and QA the month's activities, then launch each one with an agreed audience and run time.
Analyze the results of finished activities by audience, reading lift and confidence on the success metrics each plan chose.
Share readouts and next steps with stakeholders, and add new ideas to the roadmap through one repeatable intake.
deliverables: Launched A/B and Experience Targeting activities
asks: A standing monthly review with the stakeholders who act on test results
New test ideas from your teams, sent through the agreed intake
risk: A program that stalls between tests: we keep a ranked roadmap and one repeatable intake, so the next activities are ready when the last ones end.
outcome: New activities go live from your roadmap each month, and your stakeholders get readouts by audience with clear next steps.

steps: Run discovery workshops with each team to map how work is requested, planned, reviewed and delivered today, and record each process in a process map.
Agree the structure of groups, teams and job roles with your leads, and set them up in Workfront with the system preferences.
Stand up a governance board with named roles for the rollout, and agree how it decides on changes, standards and priorities.
Turn the process maps into a rollout plan that names which processes move into Workfront first and what each later step builds.
deliverables: Groups, teams, job roles and system preferences in Workfront
Governance board charter with named roles
asks: A lead from each team for the discovery workshops
Named people for the governance board, with time set aside for its meetings
Your organization chart, or a list of teams and job roles
risk: Setup that copies today's workarounds into Workfront: we map each process first and agree changes with the governance board before building.
outcome: You have mapped processes, a Workfront structure of groups, teams and job roles, and a governance board ready to steer the rollout.

steps: Agree what each audience needs to see and do, for requesters, project managers, creatives and approvers, in an access and layout plan.
Assign access levels by license type, which set the limits within which people share objects with view, contribute or manage permissions.
Build a layout template for each audience, so requesters, project managers, creatives and approvers each see the parts of Workfront they use.
Assign the templates to groups, teams and job roles with your Workfront system administrator, who makes the team and job-role assignments, then test each one.
deliverables: Access and layout plan by audience
Access levels assigned by license type
asks: Your Workfront system administrator, to make the team and job-role assignments
The list of users with their license type and audience
risk: People seeing too much or missing what they need: we test each layout template and access level as a sample user of that audience.
outcome: Each person opens Workfront with access suited to their license type and a layout built for their role, from requester to approver.

steps: List every kind of request your teams take, who submits it, who receives it and what it must include, in an intake inventory.
Set up each request queue as a project in the Queue Details area, with queue topics for the request types it takes.
Build a custom form for each request type, and add routing rules that send each request to the right user, job role, team or project.
Test sample requests of every type from submission to the receiving team, and fix forms or routing before the queues open.
deliverables: Request queues with queue topics and routing rules
Custom forms for each request type
asks: The kinds of requests each team takes today, with examples of complete requests
A lead from each receiving team to approve its form fields and routing
risk: Requests that arrive incomplete or land with the wrong team: we test sample requests of every type end to end before the queues open.
outcome: Every request is submitted the same way, arrives with what the work needs, and goes to the right team.

steps: Pick the repeatable work to template, such as campaigns, content and launches, and walk through recent real projects with the people who ran them.
Draft each project template with its tasks, durations, roles and custom forms, and agree it with the team that runs that work.
Add the approvals each template needs, using reusable approval templates with multi-stage approvals or parallel paths where the review calls for them.
Pilot each template on a live project, adjust tasks and durations from what the pilot shows, and hand over the final version.
deliverables: Project templates for the agreed repeatable work
Pilot results and template change notes
asks: Examples of recent campaign, content and launch projects, with the people who ran them
A template owner in each team to sign off its template
risk: Templates built from how work should run rather than how it does: we draft from recent real projects and pilot each template before rollout.
outcome: Your teams start repeatable work from project templates with the tasks, durations, roles, approvals and forms already in place.

steps: Plan training by role for administrators, project managers and requesters, with exercises built on your own processes and projects.
Start with one basic process, such as a simple request, and train each role on it until it runs end to end in Workfront.
Add further processes in stages once the first one runs, with short sessions for each role at every stage.
Set up regular training sessions for new and existing users, with materials your administrators can run themselves.
deliverables: Training sessions and materials for each role
Regular training schedule for new and existing users
asks: The names and roles of the administrators, project managers and requesters to train
One basic process to start with, and the team that runs it
risk: Too much change at once: we start with one basic process and add the rest in stages, so people learn on work they know.
outcome: Your administrators, project managers and requesters each use Workfront for their part of the work, and new users are trained on a regular schedule.

steps: Run the monthly administration: add and remove users, and update forms, templates and reports as your teams' work changes.
Collect user feedback on a set cadence, through short surveys and conversations with each team, and log each request.
Bring the proposed changes to the governance board each month, then make the approved ones and report back to users.
deliverables: Change proposals for the governance board
asks: A standing slot on the governance board's agenda each month
Notice of people joining, moving or leaving, from your team leads
risk: Small requests piling up until people work around Workfront: we collect feedback on a set cadence and bring changes to the board each month.
outcome: Workfront keeps up with how your teams work, with users, forms, templates and reports updated through a steady, board-approved cycle.

steps: Agree who only views experiments and who manages experiment metadata, and record each person's role and sandboxes in an access list.
Add the Experiment accelerator resource to the agreed roles with View Experiments or Manage Experiment Metadata, and assign the sandboxes each role covers.
Add the users to their roles, and test with one viewer and one manager that each sees the right experiments and permissions.
deliverables: Access list of roles, users and sandboxes
Roles with the Experiment accelerator resource
asks: The people who will view experiments and those who will manage their metadata
An administrator who can change roles and assign sandboxes
risk: People editing experiment details they should only read: we split View Experiments and Manage Experiment Metadata by role and test both.
outcome: Your team opens Experimentation Accelerator in the right sandboxes, with viewers and metadata managers each holding the access their role needs.

steps: Review how your teams test today with your marketing and analytics leads, and agree what the playbook must settle for every test.
Set the hypothesis format, covering what you are changing, what you expect to happen and why, and the primary and secondary metrics for each kind of test.
Agree how sample size and run time are set before launch, and the segmentation rules for reading results by audience.
Set up how learnings are recorded, in one learnings log your teams check before proposing a test, and hand over the playbook.
deliverables: Rules for metrics, sample size and run time
asks: Marketing and analytics leads to agree the playbook's rules
Examples of recent tests and how their results were used
risk: Tests that cannot be compared or learned from: every test follows one hypothesis format and one set of metric rules, and each result goes in one learnings log.
outcome: You have one testing playbook that sets the hypothesis format, metrics, sample size, run time and segmentation rules, and a learnings log for recording what each test teaches.

steps: List each running experiment with its owner, and gather the planned change, expected impact and treatment screenshots from each owner.
Add a hypothesis to each experiment, stating the planned change and its expected impact on the primary metric, and confirm the treatment details and screenshots.
Track which experiments have reached statistical significance and generated insights, and follow up with owners on any experiment still missing details.
asks: The owner of each running experiment, to supply its planned change and expected impact
Screenshots of each treatment, or access to the pages or messages tested
risk: Insights that never appear because details are missing: we complete every hypothesis and treatment, and track which experiments still await statistical significance.
outcome: Each running experiment carries its hypothesis and confirmed treatment details, which the accelerator needs before it generates insights and opportunities.

steps: Agree the primary metric for each experiment with its owner, matched to the hypothesis and the decision the test will drive.
Choose and import each experiment's primary metric from Customer Journey Analytics or Adobe Analytics, as a change that stays in the accelerator.
Check each experiment's results against the same metric in your reporting source, and record the metric choices in a metric register.
deliverables: Agreed primary metric for each experiment
Primary metrics imported into the accelerator
asks: The owner of each experiment, to agree its primary metric
Access to the Customer Journey Analytics or Adobe Analytics metrics you report on
risk: Judging a test on the wrong measure: we agree each primary metric against its hypothesis and check the results against your reporting source.
outcome: Each experiment in the accelerator is measured on the primary metric your team chose, drawn from the reporting source you already use.

steps: Train marketers and analysts to read experiment outcomes in the Experiments tab, including which treatment performs best and its percentage improvement over the control.
Explain insights and the Opportunities panel's AI-generated recommendations, with learning and conversion potential, and how each can be reviewed and edited before it is pushed out.
Practice sharing results using your own experiments, so each team can explain an outcome and its next step to stakeholders.
deliverables: Training sessions for marketers and analysts
Guide to reading outcomes, insights and opportunities
asks: The marketers and analysts to train, with time for a working session
A few of your own completed experiments to use in the exercises
risk: AI opportunities taken as instructions: we train people to review and edit each recommendation against your goals before acting on it.
outcome: Your marketers and analysts read experiment outcomes, insights and opportunities on their own, and share results with stakeholders in one agreed format.

steps: Review the experiments list and the KPI section each month with your team, including experiments created and in progress, and note any that stalled.
Pick the opportunities worth testing next, reviewing and editing each recommendation, and add them to the test backlog in rank order.
Record the month's finished experiments and what they taught in the learnings log, and share a short monthly summary.
asks: A standing monthly review with your testing leads
Decisions on which opportunities to test, from the owner of each area
risk: Good opportunities lost in the list: we review the experiments and opportunities every month and rank the ones worth testing in one backlog.
outcome: Your test backlog and learnings log stay current each month, with the next tests picked from reviewed opportunities and results.

steps: Agree the report suite and the pages where your images appear, and enable AEM Assets Reporting on that report suite.
Create the server-to-server credential with the Analytics API, and configure Assets Insights in AEM to read from the report suite.
Add the tracking to your pages with your web team, and check that impressions and clicks for test images reach the report suite.
Show your content team how to read the scores on each image and folder in the Insights view, using its first results.
deliverables: AEM Assets Reporting enabled on the report suite
Content team walkthrough of the Insights view
asks: An Adobe Analytics administrator to enable reporting and create the credential
A web developer to add the tracking to the agreed pages
risk: Scores that stay empty because some pages lack tracking: we test impressions and clicks on sample images before handing over.
outcome: Your content team sees impressions and clicks as scores on each image and folder in AEM Assets, read from your Adobe Analytics report suite.

steps: Agree the report suite, the pages and the interactions to track with your analytics team, and record them in a tracking plan.
Create the IMS and Analytics cloud configurations in AEM, and attach them to your site.
Set up the tags property with the Adobe Analytics extension, and build rules on the AEM data layer for page views and the agreed interactions.
Check page views and interactions in the report suite against test visits, and fix any rule that sends missing or wrong values.
deliverables: IMS and Analytics cloud configurations attached to the site
Tags property with rules on the AEM data layer
asks: An analytics contact who owns the report suite and agrees what to track
Access to AEM and the tags property for the build
risk: Data that arrives with gaps or wrong values: we test page views and interactions against known test visits before handing over.
outcome: Your AEM site sends page views and the agreed interactions to your Adobe Analytics report suite, through a tags property your team can extend.

steps: Agree the report suite and the behaviors that should start or advance a journey, such as a cart addition, with your marketing team.
Enable the Analytics source connector for the agreed report suite, so its data arrives in Adobe Experience Platform as Experience events.
Define the rule-based events and their profile identifier on the Analytics schema, and check that test visits produce the expected events.
Test the first journey they trigger with test profiles in a development sandbox, before it is activated in production.
deliverables: Analytics source connector enabled for the report suite
Rule-based events with their profile identifier
asks: The behaviors your marketing team wants journeys to respond to
An Adobe Analytics contact who owns the agreed report suite
risk: Events that fire for the wrong people or not at all: we check the profile identifier on test visits and test the journey with test profiles.
